notes: \cpara{Sets the question, prompted by comments on ``Lotteries: A Waste of Hope'' two days earlier. The comments bear out the description. One asks ``what is the standard by which you can judge someone who has the reverse preferences as behaving stupidly''; another quotes a blogger who wrote, of lottery buyers, ``don't call the consumer stupid.''}
\cpara{Offers a joke reply about utility functions, then sets it aside as ``only a snappy comeback, not an answer.''}
\cpara{The answer: the author has an interest in humanity's future, which includes the pursuit of truth. It is stated as a belief (``I believe that it is right and proper'') and not argued for.}

\cpara{This is the step ``Why Truth?'' (27 November 2006) described: ``If you think it your duty to look behind the curtain, you are a lot more likely to believe that someone else should look behind the curtain too.'' That post added: ``I tend to be suspicious of morality as a motivation for rationality.'' The trouble it named there was bad habits in one's own thinking. The safeguard this post goes on to offer concerns how others are treated.}
\cpara{Grants the danger: people have been burned for thinking wrongly. The last lines show, by irony, that condemning the burners can repeat their reasoning.}

\cpara{The proposal is the line Mill drew in \textsc{On Liberty} (1859). Of what is for a person's own good, Mill wrote: ``These are good reasons for remonstrating with him, or reasoning with him, or persuading him, or entreating him, but not for compelling him.'' The post calls it ``my proposal.''}

\cpara{Describes a rival fix: forbid judging. No one is named or quoted holding it, and its second sentence is exaggeration. The comments quoted in the first note ask by what standard the author judges, or object to one judgment; none that I found says that no one should ever judge.}
\cpara{The author's answer: keep the judgment and deny the ``therefore.'' Argue against what Susie said, but use neither violence nor regulation to stop her talking.}

\cpara{Extends the rule to the whole future: win by convincing, as science settles factual disputes ``with experiments and mathematics, not violence and edicts.'' The author calls this a principle of Rationality to which ``I have pledged my allegiance.''}

\cpara{Reads relativism as a refusal to judge. In moral philosophy the term usually names the claim that moral disagreement is deep, or that moral truth is relative to a group. The \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} (``Moral Relativism'') treats tolerance as a separate thesis; many take relativism to imply it, but ``most philosophers believe it is mistaken.'' Even tolerance, it adds, ``does not ordinarily mean indifference or absence of disapproval.'' A relativist in these senses may judge by their own standards. The charge ``they would not judge'' fits only the view that no one should judge.}

\clogic{A known objection to ethical egoism. The \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} (``Egoism'') grants that the egoist ``is unlikely to recommend ethical egoism to others,'' and adds that such worries ``do not show inconsistency.'' An egoist who argues for egoism is doing something unusual; that does not show the arguer is not an egoist.}
\cpara{Follows from the previous paragraph's definitions: anyone heard arguing for relativism or selfishness has already been counted as not a true one. It is not an observation.}

\cpara{For the case the post began with, believing what is pleasant, the final answer is modest. ``In many cases, it is a small darkness only,'' and lying to yourself in private ``does not shadow humanity's history so much'' as public lies or burnings. What remains is that the author ``cannot help but mourn,'' and the limit is repeated: argue, do not burn.}
